Love the Filters - I really like coffee but I am a huge tea drinker and love to take tea with me when I am on the go but sometimes it can be a pain to brew up a cup of my loose leaf when I need to get going in the morning. Now that I have discovered this however, it has changed things for me. I can totally put in my loose leaf tea and brew it from my Keurig. I know there are a lot of different reusable K-cup things out on the market and while many of them are great (which I own quite a few) sometimes you want a little more filtration and that is where these comes in. The filters that come with these are great and really make for a nice cup of tea, without any of the fine residue that can come from loose leaf tea but it also makes for a great smooth cup of coffee too. Either way you go, you can't go wrong with these. I keep them in my tea box for whenever I want to make a quick cup of tea for the road and the cool part is that I have even reused the filters (for the same type of tea, of course) and they can work again and again for at least to help brew up two to four more cups, at least. They might not recommend doing that, but I like to get every cent out of something and I can even help the environment too by using these, love them.

Now the cups on the other hand aren't my favorite at all. It's just like a k-cup, thin plastic. The first time you use it the Keurig will make one hole on the top and one on the bottom of the cup and in order to use it again you can either pop it in and not worry about the other hole or line it up perfectly so that no other holes are made. Yeah, to much work for a cup of tea, for me. While they work just like a k-cup, I didn't reuse them like I did the filters. I actually used the filters in a reusable k-cup that I already had which, for me, worked much better than trying to use these plastic cups. I would totally buy this for the filters but not for the cups.

No humidistat built in. - This is a pretty nice unit, but the big thing it is missing is a (rudimentary) thermostat. You basically set an analogue style switch as to how much water you want pumped out into the air, but it's really not set-and-forget the way some are: this winter is a perfect example, how in the mid-Atlantic region the outside humidity has changed a lot, and of course you don't need it on when the air is naturally at 40%+. I am pretty disappointed about that (apparently you can buy an add-on) considering this is a great brand. Everything else about it is really nice, too (except that it is bigger than some other models that can hold the same amount of water). That said, it does fill easily and it works well. It also looks better than most.

As usual, you have to change the wicks now and then (you definitely need to dry them out well on the off-season. You can soak them in a vinegar solution to cull the mold effect. I tried the wickless types, and they clog my HVAC filter with calcium deposits to the point where it stops working after just two weeks, which obviously makes those types a no-go for my house. Distilled water works, but is more expensive than wicks over time (perhaps unless you happen to have a still, although it takes time and [electric] energy to distill all the water you will need).
